pr_title: Use reset event in Kestrel heartbeat to quickly stop thread
pr_comments:
@mconnew This PR updates Kestrel heartbeat to exit immediately and stop before Kestrel starts shutting down. That removes the need to use `_stopped` to suppress error from heartbeat that you added.

Can you take a look and check that your original issue is still solved?
@Tratcher I moved heartbeat stop to the start of shutdown. Can you double check this is ok?

@JamesNK, it looks like it should resolve it as Dispose() won't return until it will no longer call OnHeartbeat. There's nothing preventing a later change bringing the issue back though as OnHeartbeat is internal so callable. In the catch block you could call WaitOne with a timeout of 0. You can then check the true/false value that's immediately returned to know if it's been set and still avoid logging. That would also enable you to keep the unit test you've removed.

Also, why not ManualResetEventSlim? ManualResetEvent allocates a native win32 handle and the Slim variant is all managed.

> OnHeartbeat is internal so callable

OnHeartbeat is only internal for unit tests. It won't be called after the heartbeat is disposed.

> Also, why not ManualResetEventSlim? ManualResetEvent allocates a native win32 handle and the Slim variant is all managed.

I read that slim implementation offers an advantage for short wait times, which doesn't apply here.

> In .NET Core and .NET 5+, the default spin-waiting duration is short: on the order of 10s of microseconds, depending on platform and processor. If you expect wait times to be much longer than that, you can still use this class instead of [ManualResetEvent](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.threading.manualresetevent?view=net-7.0) (perhaps configured with less or no spin-waiting). However, the performance benefit would likely be only marginal.

So it sounds like it doesn't matter that much, but indeed it should avoid creating the OS object unless you explicitly fetch `WaitObject` on it, as far as I can see.

PR updated to use `ManualResetEventSlim`. Set spin count to zero as we're waiting a long time (1 sec) between heartbeats. Spinning would be wasted CPU.

Added a test for the heartbeat loop. Previously wasn't tested.

issue_context.title: Exit Kestrel heartbeat thread immediately on stop
issue_context.body:
### Is there an existing issue for this?

- [X] I have searched the existing issues

### Describe the bug

Noticed in https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/pull/47580

Kestrel creates a thread and sleeps for a second in its heartbeat:

https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/blob/f295d1f75cd79c6b3abd4f27b8f4b14a58186e7a/src/Servers/Kestrel/Core/src/Internal/Infrastructure/Heartbeat.cs

When Kestrel stops there isn't a way to immediately stop the thread. `Thread.Sleep` doesn't have cancellation.

We could change it to an AutoResetEvent + OneWait(interval). When Kestrel stops the event can be triggered and exit immediately.

However, one thing to consider is making the heartbeat as reliable as possible. `Thread.Sleep` vs waiting on and event handle + timeout might have different behavior if the server is under heavy load.

### Expected Behavior

The heartbeat thread immediately exits when Kestrel is stopped.

### Steps To Reproduce

_No response_

_No response_

_No response_

comments:
we could consider switching  back to a timer now. The thread pool handles starvation better 

cc @stephentoub @kouvel
I was going to ask whether `Thread.Interrupt()` would help here. The sleep behind `Thread.Sleep()` is alertable, and Interrupt() will break into it.

> However, one thing to consider is making the heartbeat as reliable as possible. Thread.Sleep vs waiting on an event handle + timeout might have different behavior if the server is under heavy load.

Why would load affect it?

A `Timer` wasn't used here because we didn't want thread pool issues ever to impact the reliability of the heartbeat. In fact, we use the heartbeat event to alert people to thread pool starvation.

I don't know one way or the other about wait handles. Does `WaitHandle.WaitOne(TimeSpan.FromSeconds(1))` always promptly return after the timeout?

Perf probably doesn't matter since we're only waiting once a second, but I'm guessing a wait handle is a little less efficient than `Thread.Sleep`.

The difference between `Sleep` and `WaitOne` would probably be negligible in this case. If Kestrel stopping also implies the process exiting, I'm not sure what would be gained from actively shutting down the heartbeat thread. With https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/pull/47580 I imagine there could still be race conditions where the heartbeat code could run after disposal.

Typically Kestrel is stopped when the process exits, but it can be stopped without killing the process. For example, you could have unit tests that start and stop Kestrel inside each test. A bunch of idle heartbeat threads could build up as tests are running.

Yeah, https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/pull/47580 is still racey. Kestrel can be stopped anytime, including while the heartbeat is running. The only side effect will likely be a heartbeat subscriber throwing an error back to the heartbeat manager type. The `if (!_stopped) { }` check in the catch block will suppress logging that.

> I was going to ask whether `Thread.Interrupt()` would help here. The sleep behind `Thread.Sleep()` is alertable, and Interrupt() will break into it.

We have the thread reference. `Interrupt` would work. However, we'd need to catch the interrupt exception that `Thread.Sleep` throws and probably need some extra synchronization to prevent interrupts happening after `_stopped` is checked but before `Thread.Sleep`.

`ManualResetEvent.WaitOne(interval)` would have simpler code, but switching to it would be a more significant change to how the heartbeat timer works.

review_comments: total nit, I think IsAlive is redundant here.
Some unit tests call dispose without calling start. It's also possible heartbeat gets created and there is an error before start is called. `Thread.Join` breaks if the thread isn't started.
The thread should exit quickly now that delay is interrupted. Removes the chance of heartbeat running while Kestrel is disposed.
